opus-5.5.text:
I think about this question a lot, honestly. When I started Taichi during my PhD, the motivation was very personal: I was writing physics simulation code, and every time I wanted to try a new idea I had to spend weeks on low-level performance engineering, writing CUDA kernels, managing memory layouts, handling sparse data structures by hand. I felt there had to be a better way, where you could write something that looks almost like plain Python but runs at the speed of hand-tuned GPU code.

Why is it worth continuing? A few reasons.

First, the underlying problem hasn't gone away; it's become more important. Hardware keeps getting more diverse: different GPUs, Apple silicon, mobile chips, new accelerators. Most people who want to do simulation, graphics, or numerical computing are not compiler experts, and shouldn't have to be. A good programming language and compiler can absorb that complexity so people focus on their actual ideas. That's a long-term infrastructure problem, and infrastructure only becomes valuable if someone sticks with it for years.

Second, the community. Over time, a lot of people started using Taichi in ways I never imagined: researchers doing differentiable physics, artists making visual effects, students learning computer graphics for the first time, people building tools in industry. When you see someone write a beautiful fluid simulation in a hundred lines and share it, you realize the tool lowers the barrier for creativity. That feedback is very motivating.

Third, I believe in the bigger picture of what I'd call "digital content creation for everyone." Simulation and 3D content are still really hard to make. If we can make high-performance computing accessible, more people can build interactive, physical, realistic worlds, whether for games, science, education, or AI training environments.

And frankly, it's also just fun. Building a compiler and a language is one of the most intellectually satisfying things I've done. There are always hard problems: how to make it faster, more portable, easier to debug. As long as people find it useful and I keep learning, I think it's worth continuing.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that the original problem Taichi set out to solve hasn't gone away. There's still a huge gap between how people want to express computation and what actually runs fast on hardware. If you're doing physical simulation, or anything with sparse data structures, irregular access patterns, or lots of small custom kernels, you still end up choosing between writing something readable in Python that's painfully slow, or dropping into CUDA and C++ and losing weeks to tooling and debugging. Taichi was built to collapse that gap, and I don't think the gap has closed.

The second reason is that the hardware landscape has gotten more fragmented, not less. You've got NVIDIA GPUs, Apple silicon, mobile chips, various accelerators, and people want one piece of code that runs across all of them. A compiler-based approach, where you write the computation once and let the system handle backends and memory layout, becomes more valuable the more heterogeneous things get.

And then there's the community side. Over the years I've seen students, researchers, indie developers, and people in industry use Taichi to build things they just wouldn't have attempted otherwise, because the barrier to entry was too high. Fluid solvers, soft body simulation, differentiable physics, even procedural art. That's not something you walk away from lightly. When a tool lets a single grad student build something that used to take a team, you want to keep that door open.

I'd also say that the lessons from Taichi, around data-oriented design, decoupling algorithms from data layout, making differentiable simulation accessible, those ideas are still relevant to where AI and graphics are heading. Whether the project continues in exactly its current form or feeds into something new, the work is worthwhile because the ideas keep paying off.

If you’re working on simulation or graphics, you want to focus on the algorithm, but getting good performance can require a lot of low-level programming. Taichi can help reduce that burden.

What excites me is the possibility of making that kind of programming accessible to more people. If someone can test an idea quickly, see the result, and keep improving it, they can explore things they might otherwise never try. I think that’s a worthwhile problem to keep working on.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s still a lot of room to make high-performance programming easier. When you’re working on simulation, you want to spend your time thinking about the physics or the algorithm, but often you end up spending a lot of time making the code run fast on a particular device. With Taichi, the idea is to reduce that gap—to let you express what you want to compute in a relatively simple way and still get good performance.

That’s worthwhile because it can change what people are willing to try. If building and testing an idea becomes much easier, more people can experiment, including people who aren’t experts in GPU programming. For me, that’s a compelling reason to keep working on it.
